stage_state.summary_md:
## Retirement Planning and Announcement

BA wanted simultaneous retirement with Air France at end of summer schedule (October). Air France agreed, then decided to retire in May instead. This reflected their at-odds attitudes; in the shadow of the accident, a dual retirement perceived as celebratory would never be sanctioned in France.

BA planned to announce retirement at a Forum 150 meeting on 9th April 2003. Bannister pointed out this was the 34th anniversary of the first flight of the British Concorde, so the announcement moved to 10th April.

Bannister wore his uniform to signal gravitas. He presented a slide show explaining the rationale. The Marmite factor hit: roughly two-thirds of senior management expressed great sadness, the remainder relief. No one was ambivalent.

## Public Messaging

Bannister became company spokesman. Key messages: this was a commercial decision spurred by factors beyond BA's control; customers would continue to be looked after via upgraded Club Class and First on 747s.

At the press conference, a reporter asked why she was being retired. Bannister hesitated, then said: 'It's the right decision at the right time for the right reasons.' This became the universally adopted party line.

## Key Questions

'Why spend all that money getting Concorde back into the air, only to retire it less than two years later?' Answer: retirement was not due to the accident; it was for sound commercial reasons.

'Why not let Mr Branson have it?' BA anticipated this. If Virgin succeeded, Branson would say BA couldn't run a tea shop. If Virgin failed, he'd blame BA's maintenance. If BA refused, he'd claim BA was being beastly. The party response: 'Because the aeroplane was originally funded by the UK government, the decision to transfer ownership isn't ours to make.' A senior Virgin pilot told Bannister at a Guild of Air Pilots and Air Navigators event: 'You're not really going to give Concorde to us, are you, Mike?' Bannister replied 'not a chance in hell.' The pilot said 'Thank God, because it would probably send us bust!' Bannister agreed it almost certainly would have.

'Couldn't one aeroplane be retained for air shows?' This had been done with the Lancaster, Spitfires, Hurricanes of the RAF's Battle of Britain Memorial Flight, and the Avro Vulcan. But Concorde was more complex than the Vulcan. The Vulcan flew on a 'Permit to Fly' with lower certification standards because it never carried passengers. Concorde needed a 'Certificate of Airworthiness' and 'Type Certificate'. The £60 million per annum infrastructure cost was about to soar by another £40 million. Infrastructure cost didn't shrink with fleet size. Even if reduced to £50 million, that's a million a week for one aircraft. Airbus, the Type Certificate Holder, had made clear they weren't interested—their focus was on the A380 and A320 family. Airbus was under no compulsion to transfer the Type Certificate. The air-intake computer technology was proprietary and secret, used on military aircraft Airbus produced or maintained. There was no upside for Airbus: nobody would say 'Look, there goes an Airbus Concorde!'—only association if something went wrong.

## Public Sentiment Shift

As spring turned to summer, discussion shifted to Concorde's legacy. People talked about the 'wonderful job' UK plc had done. Bannister overheard conversations like 'I never got to fly on Concorde myself, sadly, but I know someone whose Aunt Mabel once flew on it and she'd had the time of her life.' The clamour for a celebration of the aircraft's life after twenty-seven years of successful operation eclipsed the doom-merchants.

BA ensured recognition for all who'd been associated with Concorde: designers, builders, flight crew, cabin crew, engineers, baggage handlers, ticket agents, and the public.

Edward de Bono told Bannister Concorde appealed to both sides of the brain—analytical and artistic—because she was technologically superb and artistically graceful. Bannister thought the reason simpler: most Brits felt a sense of ownership. 'That's my Concorde up there—something of which I can be rightly proud.'
